extracted.intended_audience: biomedical researchers (pharmacology/neuroscience/drug abuse scientists), trainees, and faculty concerned with experimental design, publication, and grant policy
extracted.subtask_short: scientific publication and experimental design standards
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and informal standards for designing, analyzing, and reporting biomedical experiments and for publication/grant-related practices; includes paraphrased journal (BJP) experimental-design requirements and practical commentary. Targets researchers preparing manuscripts, experiments, or grant/award applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori power analysis / sample size calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental design should be subjected to ‘a priori power analysis’ and a priori sample size calculation that should be included in Methods and should include alpha, power and effect size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power analysis depends on chosen effect-size estimates (pilot or prior experiments); authors can demonstrate a range of acceptable sample sizes by varying assumed effect sizes and power. Methods must include alpha, chosen power, and effect-size assumptions so reviewers/readers can judge sample-size rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum group size guidance (N ≥ 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: You should shoot for a group size of N=5 or above and if you have fewer you need to do some explaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blogger regards this as a minor burden but expects justification when smaller groups are used; provides caution that power/sample-size choices are linked to effect-size assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal group sizes for groups < 20 and explanation for variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups less than 20 should be of equal size and if there is variation from equal sample sizes this needs to be explained, particularly for exclusions or unintended loss of subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sample-size equality is violated, document reasons (e.g., exclusions, loss of subjects) and justify any imbalance in Methods/Results to satisfy reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomization of subjects and treatment order
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects should be randomized to groups and treatment order should be randomized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random assignment should be used to allocate experimental units and to sequence treatments; this is a core design requirement rather than optional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding of assignment, recording, and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment of subjects/preparations to groups, data recording and data analysis should be blinded to the operator and analyst unless a valid scientific justification is provided for not doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If blinding the operator is impossible for technical reasons, data analysis can and should be blinded. Provide valid scientific justification in the paper when full blinding cannot be performed; expect reviewer scrutiny and disagreement about what is 'impossible'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization and transformation must be justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Normalization and transformation should be well justified and follow acceptable practices (e.g., you can’t compare a treatment group to the normalization control that now has no variance because of this process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain rationale and method for any normalization or transformation in Methods; ensure transformations do not produce misleading comparisons (e.g., removing variance from controls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse analytical replicates with experimental replicates
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t confuse analytical replicates with experimental replicates in conducting analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat experimental replicates (independent experimental units) as the basis for statistical inference; analytical/technical replicates cannot substitute for biological/experimental N. Make replication type explicit in Methods and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefine and consistently apply statistical significance threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing groups, a level of probability (P) deemed to constitute the threshold for statistical significance should be defined in Methods, and not varied later in Results (by presentation of multiple levels of significance). Thus, ordinarily P < 0.05 should be used throughout a paper to denote statistically significant differences between groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the threshold (e.g., P<0.05) in Methods and consistently use it; avoid presenting multiple significance thresholds post hoc. The blogger endorses reporting a single pre-specified cutoff and criticizes inconsistent p-value reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-hoc tests only after significant omnibus ANOVA and homogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: After analysis of variance post hoc tests may be run only if F achieves the necessary level of statistical significance (i.e. P < 0.05) and there is no significant variance in homogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not run/post-hoc compare when the omnibus ANOVA is non-significant; check homogeneity of variance assumptions before running post-hoc tests. This may encourage planned-comparison strategies when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not truncate methods/figures to meet alleged initial-submission length limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Obeying the alleged word or character limits for initial submission is for suckers — shrinking down methods or figure count to meet alleged initial submission limits can put you at a disadvantage if other groups do not do that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit comprehensive methods/figures where allowed for initial submission; shortening important sections to appease alleged limits risks reviewer misunderstanding or losing competitive completeness. The post argues initial submissions should not be artificially trimmed to game length limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for and report circadian/light-cycle factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Light cycle and circadian phase matter — experimental outcomes (e.g., mortality, self-administration) can differ dramatically depending on time-of-day and light conditions; these factors affect replicability and generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to control or systematically vary circadian phase and light-cycle conditions where relevant; report animal light cycles and timing of interventions in Methods. Be aware of facility constraints (room reverse-cycling, access) and document compromises that could affect replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key research questions for e-cigarette studies (research agenda criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Important empirical questions that e-cigarette research should address: Do e-cigs help people quit smoking? Do e-cigs prolong nicotine use in individuals who would otherwise have quit? Do e-cigs cause novel harms (beyond demonstrated ingredient presence)? Do e-cigs prevent well-established harms of combustible tobacco? Do e-cigs addict new individuals? Are e-cigs used without nicotine? Are e-cigs used to deliver other psychoactive drugs?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies and reviews should be designed to inform these questions using appropriate control groups, toxicology with relevant exposures/doses, longitudinal designs where possible, and causal-inference-appropriate methods. Mere detection of an ingredient is not evidence of harm — quantify exposures and use relevant models.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is acceptable to publish multiple focused papers from one project (completerer approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing several manuscripts from a single project (e.g., multi-part series) to elaborate side themes and report more figures/data is a legitimate alternative to compressing everything into one 'complete story' for a single high-profile journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple focused manuscripts to fully report experiments, give different first-author opportunities, and make fuller data available sooner rather than forcing excessive compression into one paper and hiding material in supplemental files. The blogger contrasts this with pressure to produce single 'glamour' papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCI Predoctoral to Postdoctoral Transition Award (F99/K00) eligibility note
rubrics_metrics.description: The NCI Predoctoral to Postdoctoral Fellow Transition Award (F99/K00) is open to non-citizens on the appropriate visa; unlike NRSA pre- and post-doc fellowships, this mechanism accepts non-citizen applicants with appropriate visas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The F99/K00 is intended to encourage and retain outstanding graduate students transitioning to postdoctoral cancer-research careers; applicants should check specific RFA instructions and visa-eligibility details in the funding announcement.
